reference_drawer.title: 📖 Zeroes of a Polynomial Reference Guide
reference_drawer.description: Essential definitions, identities, graphical meaning, and degree rules:

items.rule: A zero is an x-value that makes p(x) zero.
items.example: For p(x) = x - 3, x = 3 is a zero.

items.rule: A non-constant linear polynomial ax + b has one zero.
A quadratic can have 0, 1, or 2 real zeroes.
Real zeroes are x-coordinates of x-axis intersections.
items.example: Intersections at x = -2 and x = 4 give zeroes -2 and 4.

items.rule: A degree-n polynomial has at most n real zeroes.
items.example: A cubic has at most 3 real zeroes.

items.rule: If a product is zero, at least one factor is zero.

concepts.title: 1. What is a Zero of a Polynomial?
concepts.subtitle: Input that makes output zero
concepts.summary: A real number k is called a zero of polynomial p(x) if p(k) = 0.

points.text: Definition: If p(k) = 0, then k is a zero of polynomial p(x).
Key Insight: Finding a zero means solving the algebraic equation p(x) = 0.

concepts.trap: A zero is the input value x, not the constant term of the polynomial.

concepts.title: 2. Finding Zeroes Algebraically
concepts.subtitle: Linear & Quadratic Solving
concepts.summary: For linear polynomial ax + b, zero is -b/a. For quadratic ax² + bx + c, factorise and set each factor to 0.

points.text: Quadratic Polynomial: Factorise into (x - α)(x - β) = 0 to get zeroes α and β.

concepts.trap: Never divide by variable x; always factor out common terms to avoid losing roots.

concepts.title: 3. Zero-Product Property
concepts.subtitle: Factorised Products Equal to Zero
concepts.summary: If a product of two algebraic factors is zero, at least one of the factors must equal zero.
concepts.trap: Both factors do not need to be zero simultaneously.

concepts.title: 4. Geometrical Meaning of Zeroes
concepts.subtitle: Zeroes are x-intercepts
concepts.summary: The zeroes of a polynomial p(x) are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph of y = p(x) intersects the x-axis.

points.text: x-axis Condition: On the x-axis, y = 0, so intersections satisfy p(x) = 0.
Touch Point: If the parabola touches the x-axis at 1 point, it has 1 distinct repeated zero.

concepts.title: 5. Degree and Number of Real Zeroes
concepts.subtitle: Upper Bound on Real Roots
concepts.summary: A polynomial of degree n can have at most n real zeroes.

points.text: Degree Bound: Number of real zeroes ≤ degree n.
Quadratic: A quadratic (degree 2) can have 0, 1, or 2 real zeroes.

concepts.trap: Degree n means at most n real zeroes, not always exactly n real zeroes.
